extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, literary critics, and educated readers of Romantic literature
extracted.subtask_short: criticism of poetic style and translation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive commentary on poetic composition, parody/mimicry, translation, lexicography, and reading/writing practices aimed at improving poetic and critical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just imitation requires likeness balanced by difference
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the difference which must blend with and balance the likeness, in order to constitute a just imitation’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful parody or imitation conceals wit and wisdom in the semblance of folly by keeping enough resemblance to be recognizable while introducing a balancing difference; mere slavish copying (or making something even sillier) is poor satire and indicates inferior talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of ridicule by producing an even sillier copy
rubrics_metrics.description: “the attempt to ridicule a silly and childish poem, by writing another still sillier and still more childish, can only prove ... that the parodist is a still greater blockhead than the original writer”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire requires intelligence and balance; caricature without augmenting insight only degrades the satirist and does not enhance the understanding of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as balanced components: sensibility and associative rapidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius includes profound sensibility (which alone might expose to derangement) and a more than usual rapidity of association; the due modification of each by the other constitutes genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a writer's originality or creative power, consider both intensified feeling and the facility of associative thought and how they are moderated to produce coherent genius rather than instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh and obscure construction in poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh and obscure construction is identified as a defect in poetry (illustrated by lines from Wordsworth’s early poems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity of construction and avoidance of obscurity are important virtues in verse; rhetorical effect should not be achieved at the cost of intelligibility or grammatical harshness. Example lines are given to show the offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not tell only half the fact (avoid deceptive omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deception by telling the half of a fact and omitting the other half yields a tertium quid that misleads; many libels and calumnies arise this way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers should present full contexts and avoid selective presentation that produces misleading impressions; accuracy requires balancing mutually counteracting facts rather than partial reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading should stimulate original mental activity, not passive consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the ‘devotees of the circulating libraries’ as 'beggarly day-dreaming' where the mind furnishes nothing and imagery is supplied externally by the printing-office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reading should feed the reader’s own imagination and thought; mere passive intake of formulaic fiction that substitutes for thinking is a defect both in reading habits and in the literary value of such works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilation and translation demand selection, arrangement, and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: A compilation that unites the charms of romance and history and combines excellence in translation, selection, and arrangement requires great genius in the compiler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translations/compilations not only for fidelity of individual passages but for the editor/compiler’s skill in selection, ordering, and shaping material to create a work that leaves room for reflection and keeps the imagination 'on the wing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn a language by naming objects in presence (immersion method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To acquire the language of a country in the country itself, learn all words with the objects before you and ask common people how they speak—'ask the mother in the house, the children in the lanes... and look at the moves of their mouths while they are talking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical immersion—associating words with visible objects and native usage—is recommended over relying solely on bookish/formal instruction for natural idiomatic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: New words and distinctions arise by differential usage
rubrics_metrics.description: New words form either by giving one word a general and another an exclusive use, by actual distinction of meanings, or by difference of relation; pronunciation shifts can produce new words with distinct signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexical precision grows historically as senses differentiate; when meanings are conflated, erroneous consequences follow, so coining or appropriating distinct terms can resolve equivocation and clarify thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with philosophically vague terms (e.g., 'idea')
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'idea' has vague use; historically it signified a visual abstraction (Pindar), a Platonic Form, etc., and Locke and Hume adapted it differently; such vagueness causes error and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics should define technical or philosophically loaded terms in their sense to avoid ambiguity and misinterpretation, especially when engaging with metaphysical or psychological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature authorship; allow thoughts to re-circulate
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘With the greatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty; ... what medical physiologists affirm of certain secretions applies equally to our thoughts; they too must be taken up again into the circulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not publish every thought at once; reflective reworking and time prevent intellectual fatigue and preserve vigor in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish technical terms carefully (e.g., transcendental vs transcendent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between 'transcendental' and 'transcendent' is observed by elder divines and philosophers; failure to maintain such distinctions (as in Johnson’s usage) can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain historical and technical distinctions in terminology in scholastic or philosophical writing to preserve conceptual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexicographical practice should give precise individual meanings and cross-language synonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: A new lexicon ought to give precise individual meanings in English or German and include synonyms in Latin, English, and German, instead of relying on vague or general Latin terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For useful dictionaries, prefer a ‘philosophical plan’ that supplies exact senses and multilingual synonym sets to reduce ambiguity in translation and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satiric talent requires inventive contrast, not mere copying
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The talent for mimicry seems strongest where the human race are most degraded... minds of the very lowest stamp alone satirize by copying.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate satirical writing by its inventive divergence from the original and the insight it provides, rather than by the superficiality of mimicry.
